newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian looting blast kills 27 including children.
newsitem.headline: Albanian looting blast kills 27 including children.

text.p: At least 27 people were killed, 12 of them children, when they triggered a blast while looting an underground Albanian military weapons store outside Tirana on Wednesday, police said.
Explosions continued throughout the day as heat and fire set off more munitions in the arsenal complex near this remote mountain village some 80 km (50 miles) northwest of Tirana.
"All the people that were inside the store at the time were killed," a government spokesman said.

It was still unclear exactly how the incident began but police said the villagers were rifling through the stores in a complex of caves in the mountainside for the brass casings of artillery shells to sell.
The first explosion was probably touched off by the flame from a candle igniting gunpowder spilled from the shells.

A brisk trade has sprung up in Europe's poorest nation for the brass from the shells since Albanians began looting their 1,500 military arsenals as unrest spread following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in January which many lost their life savings.
Villagers said the army had deserted the complex shortly after the unrest broke out, and local people took over its defence in response to government requests.
But they admitted to going into the arsenal to look for brass when they realised they were not to be paid for their work.
"We have killed ourselves. We were defending the tunnels against our neighbours," said Ferit Uka, a villager who lost his wife and two daughters in the blast.
"We were disappointed that they did not pay us for our work," added Seit Dishani, a former army officer from the village.
A huge fire engulfed two tunnels in the storage complex and rescue workers fought to prevent it spreading to two other tunnels nearby.
"When I go to sleep I am afraid the next day there will be something like this," a visibly moved Defence Minister Shaqir Vujaq told reporters as he comforted relatives of the victims.

Former Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha created a huge national store of light weapons and artillery during his 46-year rule, some manufactured locally and the more imported from the rest of the Soviet bloc, to assuage his pathological fear of invasion of his isolationist state.
As popular anger spread following the collapse of the pyramid schemes, crowds began to move in and loot the arsenals.
Unofficial estimates say that up to a million arms have been distributed among the 3.4 million population.

The nine-party government of national reconciliation formed in March to halt the slide towards anarchy is trying to rebuild the army, many of whose members fled as unrest swept the Balkan nation, but it remains well under strength.
Police report that frequent raids on arsenals continue as villagers stockpile arms.
Twenty people were injured last week when an arms store in the northern district of Lezhe exploded as youths tried to steal explosives.
Several hundred people have been killed in Albania since the unrest broke out at the end of February, many of them victims of accidental or revenge shootings.
Nearly 6,000 troops from an eight-nation Italian-led force have arrived in Albania in the past two weeks to secure the delivery of humanitarian aid.

The terms of the three-month United Nations mandate for the force allow the troops to secure airports, ports, roads and railways, but do not allow them to disarm Albanians or to act as a police force.
